source_text: In hoc sane loco Augustinus aculeum mortis, peccatum illud opinatur antiquum, non intellegens quid sequatur, id est: virtus peccati lex; quam legem, praeceptum quod Adae positum est, conatur asserere. Sed illa lex non fuit peccati virtus, verum peccati genus. Aliud est enim exstanti rei dare virtutem, aliud quod non exstitit procreare. Esus ergo illius arboris, si non esset interdictus, malus non fuisset; postquam autem interdictus est, et a praevaricatione usurpatus, natum est ibi ex interdicente et contemnente peccatum; quamvis non ideo data lex fuisset, ut delinqueretur; sed tamen idem faciendo, id est, de arbore comedendo, non deliquisset homo, quia bona arbor erat, nisi gustus eius a lege interdictus fuisset. Quod ergo per se pravum est, verbi gratia parricidium, sacrilegium, adulterium, et malum esse etiam sine lata lege dignoscitur, bene dicitur apud praevaricatores, qui cupientiores prohibitione redduntur, virtutem acquisisse per legem; quod vero inique non usurpatur, nisi interdicatur, genus ibi proprie, non robur ei constat a legis occasione collatum. Verum quoniam hic fui longior, huius quoque libri fine commoneo lectorem meum, ut vigilanter inspiciat, nullam in lege Dei occasionem Manichaeae impietatis offendi; sed si qua putantur ambigua, secundum regulas veritatis atque rationis et exponi posse, et iustitiae convenire non dubitet. Et illos ergo qui dicunt: Non per Christum erit resurrectio mortuorum, et istos qui asserunt aeque contra Apostolum, non nostrae naturae corpus habuisse Christum, per quod Manichaeorum scita venerantur; eodem et qui legi Dei congruat vigore damnamus.
pass_a_gloss: In this place indeed Augustine opines the sting of death that ancient sin, not understanding what follows, that is: the virtue of sin the law; which law he tries to assert as the precept which was placed on Adam. But that law was not the virtue of sin, but the genus of sin. For it is one thing to give virtue to an existing thing, another to procreate what did not exist. The eating therefore of that tree, if it had not been interdicted, would not have been evil; but after it was interdicted, and usurped from prevarication, sin was born there from the one interdicting and the one despising; although the law had not therefore been given, that it would be offended; but nevertheless by doing the same, that is, by eating from the tree, the human would not have offended, because the tree was good, unless its taste had been interdicted by the law. What therefore is crooked through itself, for example parricide, sacrilege, adultery, and is distinguished as evil even without a brought law, is well said among prevaricators, who are rendered more desirous by a prohibition, to have acquired virtue through the law; but what is not iniquitously usurped, unless it is interdicted, there properly a genus, not a strength, stands conferred on it from the occasion of the law. But because I was longer here, by the end of this book also I warn my reader, that he vigilantly inspect, that no occasion of Manichaean impiety is met in the law of God; but if any things are thought ambiguous, let him not doubt that they can both be explained according to the rules of truth and of reason, and suit justice. And those therefore who say: Not through Christ will there be a resurrection of the dead, and those who assert equally against the Apostle, that Christ did not have a body of our nature, through which they venerate the decrees of the Manichaeans; we condemn by the same vigor also which suits the law of God.

pass_b_english: In this passage Augustine thinks death’s sting is that ancient sin, failing to understand what follows: ‘Sin’s power is the law’ (1 Corinthians 15:56). He tries to identify this law as the command given to Adam. But that law was not sin’s power; it was the occasion of sin’s coming into being. Giving strength to an existing thing differs from bringing into existence what did not exist.

Eating from that tree would not have been evil if it had not been forbidden. Once forbidden and then taken through transgression, sin arose there from the encounter of prohibition and contempt. The law was not given for the purpose of wrongdoing. Nevertheless, in doing the same thing—that is, eating from the tree—the human would not have sinned, because the tree was good, unless tasting it had been forbidden by law.

What is wrong in itself—for example, murder of a parent, sacrilege, adultery—and is recognized as evil even without enacted law can rightly be said to gain strength through the law in transgressors whom prohibition makes more eager. But when an act is not wrongfully undertaken unless forbidden, the law’s occasion properly supplies its origin as sin, not its strength.

Since I have been rather lengthy here, I close this book too by reminding my reader to examine carefully and see that God’s law offers no occasion for Manichaean impiety. If any passages are thought ambiguous, let the reader not doubt that they can be explained according to the rules of truth and reason and made consistent with justice. We condemn with the same force, a force fitting God’s law, both those who say there will be no resurrection of the dead through Christ and those who equally oppose the apostle by asserting that Christ did not possess a body of our nature, thereby honoring Manichaean doctrines.
